3.text: large number of names. I know of only one family that lived in the tundra

4.text: outside of group-marriage. It was the family of a Russian creole, who had

5.text: grown up in a Chukchee family, spoke the Chukchee language, and lived

6.text: according to Chukchee customs. He was married to a Chukchee woman,

7.text: but had no companions in group-marriage. “I have a jealous heart,” he used

8.text: to tell me. “It is better that I remain alone, without companions.”

9.text: At present group-marriages are often concluded without any rite. One

10.text: man simply says to another, “Let us be companions in wives” (Mɪnñewtuˊm-
10.note: fine — looked, the print supports it

11.text: gämɪk)! After this they both exercise their rights. If a good acquaintance

12.text: solicits the formation of such a union, it is improper, even in the case of refusal,

13.text: to express it in plain words, but an evasive answer must be given. On the

14.text: other hand, cases occur where the husband is willing, but the proposed friend

15.text: is distasteful to the wife. Sometimes the husband beats his wife into sub-

16.text: mission. Frequently, however, the wife stands for her right to select friends.

17.text: I was told about one woman, who, being pressed by her husband to live

18.text: with a friend whom she disliked, preferred to take her own life.

19.text: Union through group-marriage is considered equal to a blood tie. The

20.text: children born in the families of a marriage-union are regarded as cousins, or

21.text: even as brothers and sisters. They cannot marry each other, which is natural,

22.text: for they might easily have a common father.

23.text: The strength of a group-marriage is vividly depicted thus in the tale,

24.text: The Raven and the Eagle in an Exchange Marriage: “There lived a

25.text: Raven and an Eagle. The Raven had a son. The Eagle was alone with

26.text: his wife. The Raven’s wife went to visit the Eagle. The Eagle took her

27.text: from her husband and slept with her. She bore him one son. The Raven’s

28.text: son also came, and remained, to live with his mother.” Further, it is described

29.text: how the Raven’s and the Eagle’s sons grew up and began to fly out to

30.text: hunt. During one hunt a giant Eagle caught the Eagle’s son and carried

31.text: him off. Then the Raven, the first father, hearing about it, went to the

32.text: Eagle. His wife-companion, the Eagle, sat in the sleeping-room, sorrowful.

33.text: The Raven pecked him in the shoulder. He chided him and gave him blows.

34.text: “Why did you not warn the children? Why are you sitting? Let us fly, let

35.text: us pursue!” And yet it was not his son that was lost, but the son of his

36.text: companion. Then follows a description of their search. The Raven finally

37.text: finds and rescues the Eagle’s son.

38.text: Rupture of a group-marriage is regarded as possible, but I know of no

39.text: cases where it occurred except those mentioned in accounts concerning syphi-

40.text: litics. Those syphilitics were subject to ostracism, and were excluded from

41.text: the common hearth of even the closest relations. No wonder, then, that in

42.text: those cases the ties of group-marriage were also severed.
